title: Split Decision
tagline: Pick the splitter that lights every home: not too dark, not too bright.

sources.title: ITU-T G.9807.1 (02/2023), 10-Gigabit-capable symmetric passive optical network (XGS-PON)
sources.section: Annex B, clause B.6.1, Table B.6.1
sources.claim: The standard states a PON's budget as classes of path loss: N1, from 14 dB to 29 dB, and N2, from 16 dB to 31 dB. The game states it as a launch power and a receive window instead (R7, R8). Where a path would lose less than the class minimum, the network must add optical attenuators to protect receivers.

sources.title: ITU-T G.9807.1 (02/2023), 10-Gigabit-capable symmetric passive optical network (XGS-PON)
sources.section: Annex B, clauses B.9.2.6.1 and B.9.2.8.1; Tables B.9.2, B.9.3 and B.9.4
sources.claim: The attenuation range applies between the OLT and ONU reference points and includes splices, connectors, optical attenuators and other passive devices. Paths on one PON may differ by at most 15 dB. Downstream is 1575 to 1580 nm and upstream 1260 to 1280 nm.

sources.title: ITU-T G.652 (08/2024), Characteristics of a single-mode optical fibre and cable
sources.section: Appendix I, Table I.1; clause 8, Table 2, Note 2
sources.claim: Typical link attenuation is 0.5 dB/km for 1260 to 1360 nm and 0.35 dB/km for 1565 to 1625 nm. The G.652.D cable maximum is 0.40 dB/km from 1310 to 1625 nm, plus 0.07 dB/km to extend the range to 1260 nm.

sources.title: The FOA Reference Guide: Guidelines On What Loss To Expect When Testing Fiber Optic Cables
sources.claim: A typical connector loses about 0.3 dB. TIA-568 allows up to 0.75 dB for one mated connection and 0.3 dB for a splice.

sources.title: The FOA Reference Guide: Using Attenuators With Fiber Optic Data Links
sources.claim: A receiver overloads when the cable plant loses less than a minimum. An attenuator adds the missing loss.

sources.title: TEC GR/TX/OPT-001/01/APR-12, Generic Requirements for optical splitters
sources.claim: One published set of maximum splitter insertion losses: 4.0, 7.1, 10.5, 13.8, 17.1 and 20.5 dB for 1×2 to 1×64. The game's rule of 3.5 dB for each two-way split is within about half a dB of each.

sources.title: The project owner's field practice
sources.section: Owner's reviews of 19 November 2026; decisions D11, D13 and D14 in the specification
sources.claim: The game's receive window, −28 dBm to −8 dBm at the ONT, and its launch power, +5 dBm at the OLT port: the levels the project owner has seen in deployed networks. They are planning values, not a quotation of the standard.

sources.title: ITU-T G.9807.1 (02/2023), 10-Gigabit-capable symmetric passive optical network (XGS-PON)
sources.section: Annex B, clause B.9.2.6.2, Table B.9.3
sources.claim: For the 9.95328 Gbit/s downstream direction, the OLT's mean launched power is +2 to +5 dBm in class N1 and +4 to +7 dBm in class N2. An ONU's minimum sensitivity is −28 dBm and its minimum overload −9 dBm, and the path penalty allowed is 1 dB. The game's launch power is the top of the N1 range and inside the N2 range; its dark limit equals the sensitivity; its bright limit is 1 dB above the overload figure.

rule: An ONT's optical path loss is the sum, in dB, of everything between the OLT port and that ONT: fiber, connectors, fusion splices, splitters and attenuators.
An ONT's receive level, in dBm, is the launch power at the OLT port, {launch:design}, less its path loss.
Every ONT's receive level must land inside the receive window, limits included: {dark:design} to {bright:design}.
Below {dark:design}, too little light arrives and the ONT is too dark. Above {bright:design}, too much light arrives and the ONT is too bright.
Among the designs that keep every ONT inside the window, the one that serves the most homes is the answer.
assumptions: A PON is a single fiber. Both directions share one strand from the OLT port to the ONT, so each connector and each splice is counted once.

The loss card holds the job's planning values, not measurements: fiber {fiber} per km, a connector {connector}, a fusion splice {splice}, each two-way split {splitter:2}, attenuators at the value printed on them.

The receive window, {dark:design} to {bright:design}, and the launch power, {launch:design}, are the project owner's: the levels he has seen in deployed networks. They are not quoted from the standard, whose own figures are in the source list.
Every OLT port launches the same power and every ONT has the same window. The game uses one value for each.
The ONTs drawn are the nearest and the farthest on the PON. Every other home lies between them.
leftOut: The game checks only the light an ONT receives, the downstream direction. A real design also checks the upstream direction: the ONT's own light arriving at the OLT.

The loss card's fiber value is the one for the upstream wavelength (1260 to 1280 nm). The light an ONT receives travels at the downstream wavelength (1575 to 1580 nm), where fiber loses less per km, so a real ONT at the end of a long route would receive more light than the game works out.

A real transmitter's power lies in a range. A real budget takes the weakest launch the optics allow for the dark limit and the strongest for the bright limit, and allows for a path penalty. That is how the standard arrives at its loss classes, which are narrower than the game's window.
A real budget keeps margin for repairs and ageing. The game keeps none, so every number on screen comes from an element you can see.
Reflectance, bend loss and the differences between a splitter's ports are not modeled. Neither is the standard's maximum fiber distance.
The standard also limits how far apart the losses of two paths on one PON may be. The game does not test that limit on its own; every answer in the game is within it.

levels.title: Add it up
levels.outcome: Work out one ONT's path loss and receive level, and compare the level with the dark limit of the receive window.
levels.practiced: Adding every loss on a path, small ones included, taking the total from the launch power, and testing the receive level against the dark limit.

intro: Welcome to Saguaro Valley. You design the outside plant of its new fiber network: the glass, the splitters and the connections between the provider's OLT and each customer's ONT.
A PON runs on a single fiber. Light travels both ways on the same strand, from the OLT port through the splitters to the ONT, so every connector and splice you count here is on that one fiber.

Light leaves the OLT port and loses strength at everything it passes. Each loss is counted in decibels (dB), and decibels simply add up. The total from the OLT port to one ONT is that ONT's optical path loss.

The strength of the light itself is a level, counted in dBm. The OLT port launches it at {launch:design}. Take the path loss away from the launch power and you have the ONT's receive level. At an ONT that level is a negative number, and more loss makes it more negative: lower on the scale, and darker.

An ONT works only inside its receive window, which on this network is {dark:design} to {bright:design}. In this level you need only the dark end: below {dark:design} too little light arrives, and the ONT is too dark.

A splitter shares one fiber among many homes, and that sharing is the largest loss on the path. More homes on one OLT port means a cheaper network, so the question is always the same: what is the largest splitter the farthest home can carry?

The loss card, the launch power and the receive window are this job's planning values. The game uses one launch power and one fiber value, and keeps no spare margin; a real design allows for the spread of real transmitters, uses the fiber loss at each wavelength and keeps some margin. Model and sources, at the top of the page, lists everything that is left out.

terms.meaning: Optical line terminal: the provider's end of the PON. One OLT port lights one PON.
Optical network terminal: the box at the customer's end. The standard calls it an ONU.
A passive device that divides the light on the fiber among several outputs. A 1:32 splitter serves 32 homes and costs {splitter:32} on the loss card.
A place where two fiber ends plug together in an adapter, as at a patch panel or at the ONT. It is one connection on the single fiber: {connector} each.
Two lengths of the fiber fused end to end: {splice} each.
Decibel. A loss in dB adds to the other losses on the same path.
A light level: decibels counted from one milliwatt. A level in dBm less a loss in dB is again a level in dBm.
The level of the light that reaches an ONT: the launch power at the OLT port, {launch:design}, less the path loss.
The weakest and the strongest light an ONT can work with: {dark:design}, its dark limit, to {bright:design}, its bright limit.

example.title: Worked example: one home, {km:X} out, on a {ratio:x1} splitter
example.result: The path loses {total:X}. {launch} less {total:X} is {rx:X}. That is {margin:X} above the dark limit of {dark}, so ONT X is inside the window.

rounds.title: Mesquite Lane
rounds.story: A new street at the far edge of the valley, {km:A} of fiber from the OLT. ONT A is the farthest home this splitter will serve, so it is the one to budget for.
rounds.goal: Choose the largest splitter that keeps ONT A inside the window.

options.label: {ratio:s1} splitter
options.note: Careful and correct, but it leaves light unused. When a design fits with room to spare, test the next size up.

options.label: {ratio:s1} splitter
options.note: This choice usually comes from counting only the fiber and the splitter. Those two alone lose {bigOnly:A}, which this network could carry. The connectors and splices add {small:A}, and that takes ONT A below the dark limit.

hints: List everything between the OLT port and ONT A, then add the losses: fiber at {fiber} per km, connectors at {connector} each, splices at {splice} each, plus the splitter. Take the total from the launch power, {launch}, and compare the result with the dark limit, {dark}.

Before the splitter, ONT A's path already loses {fixed:A}: fiber {fiber:A} + connectors {connectors:A} + splices {splices:A}. Add each splitter's loss from the loss card, take each total from {launch}, and see which receive levels stay at or above {dark}.
rounds.explain: The path loses {fixed:A} before the splitter. With the {answer} it loses {total:A}, so ONT A receives {rx:A}: inside the window. No larger option fits.

rounds.title: Ocotillo Ranch Road
rounds.story: The same kind of street as Mesquite Lane, but closer in: {km:A} of fiber from the OLT. ONT A is the farthest home this splitter will serve.
rounds.goal: Choose the largest splitter that keeps ONT A inside the window.

options.label: {ratio:s1} splitter
options.note: It works, with a lot of light to spare. A shorter route leaves room for a bigger split, so test the larger sizes before you settle.

options.label: {ratio:s1} splitter
options.note: It works, and it was the right size for the longer route. This route loses less on the way, so the same splitter leaves light unused here. Test the next size up.

hints: A shorter route spends less light on fiber. Add the fiber, the connectors, the splices and the splitter for ONT A, take the total from {launch}, and compare the result with {dark}. Do not assume that what fitted the last street is the most this one can carry.

Before the splitter, ONT A's path loses {fixed:A}: fiber {fiber:A} + connectors {connectors:A} + splices {splices:A}. Start with the largest splitter on the loss card and check whether the receive level stays at or above {dark}.
rounds.explain: This route loses {fixed:A} before the splitter, less than Mesquite Lane did. With the {answer} it loses {total:A} and ONT A receives {rx:A}: inside the window, with {margin:A} to spare before the dark limit. Nothing larger is on offer.

levels.title: The farthest home sets the limit
levels.outcome: Apply the receive window to every ONT on a PON and compare competing designs.
levels.practiced: Budgeting for the highest-loss ONT, and adding the losses of splitters in series.

intro: One splitter serves many homes, and each home has its own path: the same OLT port, the same splitter, a different drop. Every one of those ONTs has to receive a level inside the window.

You do not have to work out all of them. The ONT with the most fiber, connectors and splices has the highest loss, and so the lowest receive level. If that ONT is at or above the dark limit, so is every ONT with less loss.
The launch power and the window are the same as before: {launch:design} at the OLT port, and {dark:design} to {bright:design} at each ONT.

Splitters can also be put in series: a small one at a cabinet feeding larger ones nearer the homes. The homes multiply, so a 1:4 followed by a 1:16 serves 64. The losses add: {splitter:4} + {splitter:16}. Splitting in two stages does not save light. You pay for both.

terms.meaning: The fiber from the OLT port to the first splitter. Every home on the PON shares it.
The last piece of fiber, from a splitter to one home.
Splitters in series. Multiply the ratios to count the homes; add the losses.

example.title: Worked example: two homes behind a {ratio:x1} splitter
example.result: ONT X loses {total:X} and receives {rx:X}. ONT Y, the farther one, loses {total:Y} and receives {rx:Y}. Both are inside the window of {window}. ONT Y is {margin:Y} above the dark limit, and that is all the room there is for a bigger split.

rounds.title: Palo Verde Loop
rounds.story: A loop road with homes spread along it. ONT A is beside the splitter, ONT B is partway round, and ONT C is the farm at the far end.
rounds.goal: Choose the largest splitter that keeps every ONT inside the window.

options.label: {ratio:s1} splitter
options.note: Every home is comfortably inside, which is the sign that a larger splitter may fit. Test the next size against the farthest ONT.

options.label: {ratio:s1} splitter
options.note: Budget for the farthest home, not a typical one. A design is only as good as its highest-loss path.

hints: All three ONTs share the feeder and the splitter. Find the ONT with the highest loss before the splitter, and budget for that one.

Before the splitter the paths lose {fixed:A} (ONT A), {fixed:B} (ONT B) and {fixed:C} (ONT C). Add each splitter to the largest of the three, take the total from {launch}, and compare the result with {dark}.
rounds.explain: ONT C is the one that matters: it loses {fixed:C} before the splitter. With the {answer} it loses {total:C} and receives {rx:C}, inside the window. ONT A and ONT B lose less, so they receive more light and are inside it too.

rounds.title: Cholla Crossing
rounds.story: A newer subdivision, split in two stages: one splitter at the cabinet, then a {ratio:s2} at each pedestal. ONT A is the home nearest its pedestal and ONT B the farthest.
rounds.goal: Choose the first-stage splitter that serves the most homes with every ONT inside the window.

options.label: {ratio:s1} first stage, then the {ratio:s2}
options.note: Homes multiply across the stages, and losses add. Both splitters are on every path.

options.label: {ratio:s1} first stage, then the {ratio:s2}
options.note: It fits with room to spare. A larger first stage multiplies the homes; check whether the farthest ONT can carry it.

hints: Stage losses add. Every path here crosses the first-stage splitter you choose and the installed {ratio:s2}.

With the installed {ratio:s2} already counted, the paths lose {fixed:A} (ONT A) and {fixed:B} (ONT B). Add each first-stage splitter to the larger of the two, take the total from {launch}, and compare the result with {dark}.
rounds.explain: The two stages together cost {chosen:B} + {installed:B}. On top of the fiber, connectors and splices, that makes ONT B's loss {total:B} and its receive level {rx:B}, inside the window. A larger first stage would take it below {dark}.

levels.title: Too much light
levels.outcome: Recognize an ONT that receives too much light and correct it with attenuation in the right place.
levels.practiced: Testing a receive level against the bright limit as well as the dark limit, and putting an attenuator where the excess light is.

intro: So far the danger was too little light. The window also has a bright end. An ONT's receiver is built to pick up a faint signal from far away, and a signal that arrives too strong overloads it.

On this network the bright limit is {bright:design}. An ONT that receives more than that is too bright. It takes a short route and a small split: a few shops beside the OLT cabinet, or a business connected ahead of the main splitter.
The cure is an attenuator: a small fixed device that adds a known loss. The standard requires one wherever a path would lose too little to protect the receiver.
Where it goes matters. At the OLT port it dims every ONT on the PON. At one ONT it dims only that ONT.

terms.meaning: A passive device that adds a fixed loss, printed on it, to everything that passes through it.
A receive level above the window's bright limit: too much light reaches the receiver.
A receive level below the window's dark limit: too little light reaches the receiver.

example.title: Worked example: an office beside the OLT, with a {att:olt} attenuator
example.result: Without the attenuator this path would lose only {fixed:X}, and ONT X would receive {drawn:X}: above the bright limit of {bright}. The attenuator adds {chosen:X}. The loss becomes {total:X} and the receive level {rx:X}, inside the window.

rounds.title: Ironwood Court
rounds.story: Four shops share a remote OLT cabinet on their corner. A {ratio:s1} splitter is already installed, so every option serves the same 4 customers. ONT A is the shop beside the cabinet and ONT B the one at the far end of the row.
rounds.goal: Choose the design that puts every ONT inside the window.

options.label: Build it as drawn
options.note: Short routes feel safe because nothing is lost on the way. That is the problem: less loss is not always safer.

options.label: Add a {att:olt} attenuator at the OLT port
options.note: The right idea, and not enough of it. The receive level has to come down to the bright limit, not just move toward it.

options.label: Add a {att:olt} attenuator at the OLT port
Add a {att:olt} attenuator at the OLT port
options.note: An attenuator can overshoot. Too much added loss turns a path that was too bright into one that is too dark.

hints: Add up each path and take it from {launch} as before, then compare the receive level with both ends of the window: {bright} and {dark}.
As drawn, the paths lose {fixed:A} (ONT A) and {fixed:B} (ONT B), so the ONTs receive {drawn:A} and {drawn:B}. An attenuator at the OLT port lowers both levels by its value.
rounds.explain: As drawn the paths lose only {fixed:A} and {fixed:B}, and the ONTs receive {drawn:A} and {drawn:B}: too bright. The attenuator adds {chosen:A} of loss to each, which brings them down to {rx:A} and {rx:B}: below {bright} and well above {dark}.

rounds.title: Agave Works
rounds.story: Agave Works, a workshop beside the splitter cabinet, takes one leg of a {ratio:s1} splitter directly. The other leg feeds a {ratio:s2} for the neighborhood. ONT A is the workshop, and ONT B is the farthest of the 32 homes.
rounds.goal: Choose the design that puts every ONT inside the window.

options.label: Add a {att:olt} attenuator at the OLT port
options.note: An attenuator at the OLT port sits on every path. It dims the bright ONT, and it dims every other ONT by the same amount.

options.label: Add a {att:A} attenuator at ONT A
Add a {att:B} attenuator at ONT B
options.note: The attenuator belongs on the path with too much light. Here it went on the other path, the one that was already the darker of the two.

options.label: Build it as drawn
options.note: A PON is not finished when its farthest home works. The window applies to every ONT, the nearest included.

hints: Work out each ONT's receive level as drawn, and note where it sits against the window. Then ask which ONTs each attenuator would affect.
As drawn, ONT A loses {fixed:A} and receives {drawn:A}; ONT B loses {fixed:B} and receives {drawn:B}. Compare each level with {bright} and {dark}.
rounds.explain: ONT A crosses only the {ratio:s1}, so its path loses just {fixed:A} and it receives {drawn:A}: too bright. The attenuator at ONT A adds {chosen:A} to that path alone. That brings ONT A down to {rx:A} and leaves ONT B at {rx:B}.
